newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Marks & Spencer slides as profits disappoint.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Marks & Spencer slides as profits disappoint.

text.p: Marks & Spencer saw its shares slide steeply on Tuesday as the British retailer's first half results fell short of market forecasts.

An increase in costs of about 8.4 percent associated with hiring 2,000 extra staff in Britain over the current year meant profits came in 20 to 30 million pounds lower than expected, retail analysts said.
The shares fell 21 pence to 488 pence and analysts downgraded full year forecasts for the retailing group.

Pretax profits in the half year to September 28 rose to 430.1 million pounds ($710.8 million) from 385.4 million. But the market had expected profits of about 450 million pounds, with some estimates as high as 460 million.
Sales rose nine percent to 3.53 billion pounds. The dividend was up 10 percent to 3.3 pence.

Investors had expected bumper profits from stores sector leader Marks because Britain's retail economy was booming. But retail analysts pointed out that Marks was not highly geared to economic recovery.

"It's a company that is not highly operationally geared. When consumer spending improves you don't see a massive gearing of profit to that," said John Richards, retail analyst at NatWest Markets. He cut his full year forecast to 1.12 billion pounds from 1.15 billion.
Chairman Sir Richard Greenbury told a news conference the group was increasing its cost base through additional staffing to improve customer service.
He described some of the market's profit expectations as "naive" and said Marks was not a recovery stock. "We're not a recovery situation, we started off being rather profitable."

The group is taking on 2,000 extra staff over the current financial year, which started in April. A fraction of the total will be used to staff three percent extra selling space coming onstream in Britain during the year.
Deputy chairman Keith Oates said the investment would also cover systems to ensure availability of merchandise when customers wanted it.
Greenbury said in a statement that consumer confidence seemed to be returning in Britain, where sales were up by 8.4 percent to 221 million pounds.
"We have increased our market share in clothing, and have held our position in foods. We have maintained our margins across the business," he said.
Home furnishings benefited from the upturn in the British housing market, with sales up 27 percent. In foods, sales rose 6.6 percent to 1.23 billion pounds.
Greenbury said Marks, which already sells home furnishings via a catalogue, was looking into expanding mail order, but had not taken a decision yet.
"We do everything very slowly," Greenbury said, "Marks and Spencer is a tortoise."
Overseas sales, including franchises, rose 12 percent to 591 million pounds, while profits were up 36 percent to 17 million.
New management at Brooks Brothers produced a turnaround to a profit of 1.1 million pounds after a loss of 2.5 million last time.
In Europe, profits were 11 million pounds, up 42 percent. But after pre-opening costs of 6.8 million profits were actually lower at 4.4 million against 6.1 million last time.
Greenbury said Marks would double its presence in Spain in the next two years and further strengthen its position in France. ($1=.6051 Pound)
